title: Tuning and Temperament
intro: How exactly should the notes of a scale be tuned? Pure intervals from the harmonic series cannot all fit into one keyboard, so every tuning system is a compromise. This chapter starts with just intonation and the commas that break it.

blocks.text: Just intonation tunes intervals to small whole-number ratios: octave 2/1, fifth 3/2, fourth 4/3, major third 5/4, minor third 6/5. A just major scale builds three just major triads (4:5:6) on I, IV and V:

blocks.caption: The just major scale (ratios to the tonic).

blocks.text: Those triads beat-free and glow; choirs, string quartets and barbershop quartets tune towards them by ear. But the scale has two sizes of whole step, 9/8 (204 cents) and 10/9 (182 cents), and the fifth from D to A is 40/27 (680 cents), badly out of tune. The ii chord of a just C major scale is unusable.

Four pure fifths up from C give E (two octaves up): $(3/2)^4 = 81/16$, against the just major third $5/4 = 80/16$ two octaves down. The difference, 81/80 ≈ 21.5 cents, is the syntonic comma. It is why pure fifths and pure thirds cannot coexist in a fixed scale.

Twelve pure fifths overshoot seven octaves by $3^{12}/2^{19} \approx 23.46$ cents, the Pythagorean comma (see the circle of fifths (#/arts/music-theory/scales-and-keys/circle-of-fifths)). Pythagorean tuning, built entirely from pure fifths, has excellent fifths but harsh major thirds (81/64, 408 cents, 22 cents wider than pure), and one 'wolf' fifth where the leftover comma lands.

widget.title: Just and Pythagorean intervals against equal temperament

blocks.text: The just major third (step 4) is 13.7 cents narrower than the equal-tempered one and the just major sixth (step 9) 15.6 cents narrower; the just minor third (step 3) is 15.6 cents wider. The Pythagorean major third is 7.8 cents wider than equal and the Pythagorean minor third 5.9 cents narrower. Fifths and fourths differ by only about 2 cents in either system.

widget.title: Hear the difference: C major triad in three tunings (switch Tuning, then play)

blocks.text: A piano cannot change tuning as it plays, which is why keyboard instruments drove the history of temperament: singers and string players adjust each note by ear, but a harpsichord or piano needs one fixed tuning that works in every key it will play in. Piano strings also have slightly sharp, inharmonic upper partials (from the stiffness of the wire), so tuners stretch the octaves, making high notes a little sharp and low notes a little flat, so the partials line up.

blocks.title: Commas
blocks.text: Compute the syntonic comma in cents.

blocks.title: Wolf
blocks.text: In a C-based Pythagorean tuning with eleven pure fifths from E♭ up to G♯, how big is the remaining 'fifth' G♯–E♭, in cents?
solution: The twelve fifths must add to seven octaves (8400 cents). Eleven pure fifths are 11 × 701.955 = 7721.51 cents, so the last is 8400 − 7721.51 = 678.49 cents: a pure fifth minus the Pythagorean comma (701.96 − 23.46). That is the wolf.
